subject: physics

items.q: In physics, what is meant by a system?
items.correct: An object or a group of objects.
items.misconception: A machine that transfers energy.
items.why: The word 'system' is used in everyday life for heating systems, sound systems and computer systems, all of which are built devices. In physics the word is deliberately much wider. The specification defines it in one line: a system is an object or group of objects. You choose the system; nothing has to be manufactured for it to count.
items.random_wrong: A group of objects, never just one.

items.q: The specification says there are changes in the way energy is stored when a system changes. Which statement describes this correctly?
items.correct: Some stores empty while other stores fill up.
items.misconception: Energy is gradually used up as the system changes.
items.why: Everyday language talks about 'using energy' and 'running out of energy', and the useful effect really does disappear. What runs out is the energy in one particular store, not the energy itself. When a system changes, some stores empty and others fill. The specification's phrase is 'changes in the way energy is stored'.
items.random_wrong: Energy is changed into a different type of energy.

items.q: Which of these is an energy store?
items.correct: The kinetic store of a moving trolley.
items.misconception: Heating a beaker of water with a flame.
items.why: Primary and lower-secondary teaching often uses a list of 'types of energy', and the phrase 'changes into' is hard to unlearn. Separate the two ideas. Stores hold energy; transfers move it. Sound, light, heating and a current flowing are transfers, not stores. A description should say which store emptied, which store filled, and by which route.
items.random_wrong: A current flowing through a heater wire.

items.q: A ball rolls down a slope. Which description best meets the requirement to describe all the changes in the way energy is stored?
items.correct: The gravitational store empties; the kinetic and thermal stores fill.
items.misconception: Gravitational potential energy changes into kinetic energy.
items.why: Primary and lower-secondary teaching often uses a list of 'types of energy', and the phrase 'changes into' is hard to unlearn. Separate the two ideas. Stores hold energy; transfers move it. Sound, light, heating and a current flowing are transfers, not stores. A description should say which store emptied, which store filled, and by which route.
items.random_wrong: Energy is transferred from the top of the slope to the bottom.

items.q: A ball is thrown vertically upwards. Which describes the changes in the way energy is stored as it rises?
items.correct: The kinetic store empties and the gravitational potential store fills.
items.misconception: The gravitational potential store empties and the kinetic store fills up.
items.why: Students associate 'most energy' with 'fastest', and do not separate the two stores; leaving the hand feels like the moment of greatest effort. The gravitational potential store depends on height, not speed. At launch the ball is low and fast, so its kinetic store is at its largest; at the top it is high and stationary, so its gravitational potential store is at its largest.
items.random_wrong: The kinetic store and the gravitational potential store both keep filling.

items.q: At the highest point of its flight, a ball thrown straight upwards is momentarily at rest. What is true of its energy stores at that moment?
items.correct: Its gravitational store is at its largest and its kinetic store is empty.
items.misconception: Its kinetic store still holds energy, or it could not fall back down.
items.why: Students link 'having energy' with 'being able to move next', and it feels as though the throw must still be pushing the ball. What brings the ball back down is the weight acting on it, not a leftover kinetic store. At the top the gravitational potential store is full; on the way down that store empties and the kinetic store fills again.
items.random_wrong: Its gravitational store is empty because it has stopped moving up.

items.q: A moving trolley crashes into a wall and stops. Which describes the main change in the way energy is stored?
items.correct: The kinetic store empties into thermal stores of both objects.
items.misconception: The kinetic store of the trolley is destroyed by the wall impact.
items.why: The motion visibly ends, and nothing obvious appears in its place, so 'destroyed' seems to describe what happened. The motion ends, but the energy does not. Crumpled metal, warm brakes, a warm wall and a bang are all evidence of stores that filled. Describing the change means naming those stores.
items.random_wrong: The kinetic store passes into the kinetic store of the wall itself.

items.q: A cyclist rides into a hedge and stops. A student says all the energy has gone into the hedge. Why is this description incomplete?
items.correct: Thermal stores of the cyclist, bike and surroundings also fill.
items.misconception: A hedge cannot store energy because a hedge does not move.
items.why: Kinetic energy is usually met first, and 'energy' is popularly associated with activity and movement. Motion fills only one store. A hot wall, a stretched spring, a lump of coal and a book on a high shelf all hold energy while completely still, and their stores can gain energy in a collision.
items.random_wrong: The cyclist's kinetic store is used up, not transferred at all.

items.q: A constant horizontal force pushes a box along a very smooth floor. Which describes the change in the way energy is stored?
items.correct: Work done by the force fills the kinetic store of the box.
items.misconception: The kinetic store of the box stays the same as it keeps moving.
items.why: 'Constant' is read as 'steady', and everyday pushing of heavy objects at walking pace really does give constant speed, because friction balances the push. Constant force means unchanging force, not unchanging speed. With no opposing force the trolley accelerates, and the work done by the force — force × distance — keeps filling the kinetic store.
items.random_wrong: The gravitational store of the box fills as it is pushed.

items.q: The same constant force accelerates a trolley over twice the distance. How does this change the energy transferred to the kinetic store?
items.correct: It doubles, because work done is force times distance.
items.misconception: It stays the same, because the force has not changed.
items.why: The everyday meaning of 'work' is effort, and applying a force certainly takes effort. The specification defines work done = force × distance (along the line of action of the force). If the distance is zero, the work done on the object is zero, no matter how big the force.
items.random_wrong: It halves, because the force is spread over more distance.

items.q: A driver brakes and the car slows down. Which describes the changes in the way energy is stored?
items.correct: The kinetic store empties and thermal stores of the brakes fill.
items.misconception: The kinetic store empties and is used up by the brakes.
items.why: Everyday language talks about 'using energy' and 'running out of energy', and the useful effect really does disappear. What runs out is the energy in one particular store, not the energy itself. When a system changes, some stores empty and others fill. The specification's phrase is 'changes in the way energy is stored'.
items.random_wrong: The kinetic store is destroyed by the friction in the brakes.

items.q: A few minutes after a car has braked and stopped, its brakes have cooled back down. What has happened to the energy?
items.correct: It has been transferred to thermal stores in the surroundings.
items.misconception: It has been destroyed as the brakes cooled down again afterwards.
items.why: Everyday language talks about 'using energy' and 'running out of energy', and the useful effect really does disappear. What runs out is the energy in one particular store, not the energy itself. When a system changes, some stores empty and others fill. The specification's phrase is 'changes in the way energy is stored'.
items.random_wrong: It has gone back into the kinetic store of the car that stopped.

items.q: Water is brought to the boil in an electric kettle. Which describes the changes in the way energy is stored?
items.correct: Work is done as a current flows; the water's thermal store fills.
items.misconception: The electrical store of the kettle empties into the water.
items.why: Phrases such as 'electrical energy' and 'using electricity' are everywhere, and a charged battery does behave like a store — but it is a chemical store. The current is the route, not the store. Work is done when a current flows, and that fills a store somewhere else — usually a thermal store or a kinetic store in a motor.
items.random_wrong: The chemical store of the water fills up as it gets hotter.

items.q: A kettle boils a full jug of water. Which statement about where the energy ends up is correct?
items.correct: Most goes to the water's thermal store, some to the kettle and room.
items.misconception: All of it goes into the thermal store of the water inside the kettle.
items.why: The intended effect is the only one that gets mentioned, and the other transfers are small and hard to see. A kettle body is warm after boiling, and steam leaves the spout — both are stores that filled. Describing all the changes means listing these as well as the water.
items.random_wrong: All of it is used up in making the water change into steam.

items.q: A kettle heats 0.50 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C. Using ΔE = m c Δθ, which is given on the Physics equation sheet, how much energy is transferred to the thermal store of the water?
items.why: The final temperature is the number the question is 'about', and the Greek letter delta is unfamiliar, so it gets ignored. The Δ symbol means 'change in'. Subtract the starting temperature from the final one: 100 − 20 = 80 °C. Using 100 would give an answer far too large.

items.q: 0.40 kg of cooking oil is heated from 20 °C to 70 °C. The specific heat capacity of the oil is 2000 J/kg °C. How much energy is transferred to the thermal store of the oil?
items.why: The final temperature is the number the question is 'about', and the Greek letter delta is unfamiliar, so it gets ignored. The Δ symbol means 'change in'. Subtract the starting temperature from the final one: 100 − 20 = 80 °C. Using 100 would give an answer far too large.

items.q: A constant force of 20 N moves a box of mass 4.0 kg a distance of 3.0 m along the line of action of the force. How much work is done by the force?
items.why: Mass appears in most other energy equations the students have met, and questions often supply a mass, which looks like an instruction to use it. W = F s uses only the force and the distance moved along its line of action. A mass given in a work-done question is often there for a different part of the question, or as a check that you know what to ignore.

items.q: A student holds a heavy box completely still, at arm's length, for 30 s. How much work is done by the student on the box?
items.correct: None, because the box does not move in the direction of the force.
items.misconception: A large amount, because a big force is needed to hold the box up.
items.why: The everyday meaning of 'work' is effort, and applying a force certainly takes effort. The specification defines work done = force × distance (along the line of action of the force). If the distance is zero, the work done on the object is zero, no matter how big the force.
items.random_wrong: It depends on the time, because holding it for longer is harder.

items.q: An electric heater has a power of 2000 W and is switched on for 3.0 minutes. Using P = E/t, how much energy is transferred by the heater?
items.why: The number in the question is 3, and the unit is not treated as part of the quantity. A watt is a joule per second, so t must be in seconds for the answer to be in joules. 3.0 minutes × 60 = 180 s, giving 360 000 J rather than 6000 J.

items.q: A current flows through the heating element of a kettle. Which statement describes what is happening?
items.correct: Work is done, and the thermal store of the element fills.
items.misconception: Electrical energy is stored in the element as current flows.
items.why: Phrases such as 'electrical energy' and 'using electricity' are everywhere, and a charged battery does behave like a store — but it is a chemical store. The current is the route, not the store. Work is done when a current flows, and that fills a store somewhere else — usually a thermal store or a kinetic store in a motor.
items.random_wrong: The current is used up as it passes through the hot element.

items.q: While boiling water, a kettle element transfers 180 000 J. Of this, 168 000 J fills the thermal store of the water and 9 000 J fills the thermal store of the kettle body. On a common scale, how much is shown transferred to the surroundings?
items.why: The intended effect is the only one that gets mentioned, and the other transfers are small and hard to see. A kettle body is warm after boiling, and steam leaves the spout — both are stores that filled. Describing all the changes means listing these as well as the water.

items.q: A bar chart on a common scale shows the energy in each store of a system before and after it changes. What should be true of the bars?
items.correct: The bars after add up to the same total as the bars before.
items.misconception: The bars after add up to less, because energy is used up.
items.why: The diagram is treated as a picture of what happened rather than as a set of calculated numbers that must balance. The point of the common scale is that the joules can be added. Work out each change in joules, and check that the amounts afterwards total the amount you started with — that is what 'redistributed' means.
items.random_wrong: Every bar after the change is smaller than it was before.

items.q: Can a single object on its own be a system?
items.correct: Yes. The definition allows an object or a group of objects, so one ball on its own is a perfectly good system.
items.misconception: A system has to be more than one thing, because things have to interact for anything to happen.
items.why: Most worked examples involve two or more objects, and the word 'group' in the definition is the part students remember. Read the definition carefully: 'an object or group of objects'. Both are allowed. Choosing a single object as the system is often the simplest way to describe a change.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When a moving object hits an obstacle, does all the energy go into the obstacle?
items.correct: No. Thermal stores of the moving object, of the obstacle and of the surroundings all fill, and sound waves carry some energy away.
items.misconception: The energy is passed on to the thing that was hit, in the same way a ball passes motion to another ball.
items.why: Collisions between snooker balls, where motion really is passed on, are the model students carry into every collision. Only when the obstacle moves off does its kinetic store fill. When an object hits a wall or a hedge and stops, the change is mostly into thermal stores on both sides of the collision plus sound.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do the brakes destroy the kinetic energy of a car?
items.correct: No. Friction forces in the brakes do work, transferring energy from the kinetic store of the car into the thermal store of the brakes.
items.misconception: Braking gets rid of the energy — the friction cancels it out.
items.why: The word 'friction' is taught as something that opposes and reduces motion, so it is easy to treat it as removing energy from existence. Friction is a force, and forces do work: they move energy between stores. Racing car brakes glow red hot, which is direct evidence of the thermal store filling.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: After a car has stopped, where does the energy in the hot brakes go?
items.correct: The brakes cool down, transferring energy to the thermal store of the surroundings.
items.misconception: The energy stays in the brakes, because that is where it went when the car stopped.
items.why: Students stop the description at the moment the car stops, and the later cooling is slow and invisible. 'All the changes' includes what happens afterwards. Anything hotter than its surroundings transfers energy to them until the temperatures match, so the thermal store of the surroundings finishes larger.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can the mass be left out of ΔE = m c Δθ if you know the substance?
items.correct: No. Specific heat capacity is the energy needed per kilogram, so the mass must be multiplied in.
items.misconception: The specific heat capacity already tells you about the water, so multiplying by 4200 and the temperature change is enough.
items.why: The word 'specific' is not read as 'per kilogram', so c looks like a property that covers the whole sample. c = 4200 J/kg °C means 4200 joules for each kilogram for each degree. Heating 0.5 kg needs half as much as heating 1 kg, so the mass has to appear in the calculation.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can an energy change caused by heating be compared with one caused by work done by a force?
items.correct: Yes. Both are energy changes measured in joules, so they can be drawn on the same scale and added.
items.misconception: Heating and work done by forces are different kinds of thing, so their values cannot be put on one scale.
items.why: The two are calculated with different equations and taught in different lessons, so they feel like different quantities. Different routes, same quantity. ΔE = m c Δθ, W = F s and E = P t all give an answer in joules, which is exactly why a single common scale works.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is 'energy is transferred' a full description of a change in a system?
items.correct: No. You must say which store empties, which store or stores fill, and how the energy was transferred.
items.misconception: Saying that energy is transferred, or that it moves from one place to another, answers the question.
items.why: The phrase sounds like correct physics vocabulary, and it is often accepted in class discussion. The specification asks for all the changes in the way energy is stored. Name the stores: for a ball rolling down a slope, the gravitational potential store empties while the kinetic store and thermal stores fill.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: You hold a heavy box still at arm's length for 30 s. How much work do you do on the box?
items.correct: None. The box does not move along the line of action of the force, so no work is done on it.
items.misconception: Holding it is exhausting and gets harder the longer you hold it, so a lot of work must be being done on the box.
items.why: Muscles really do empty a chemical store while holding a load, so the effort is genuine — it just is not work done on the box. Distinguish the two systems. Inside your arm, energy is transferred as muscle fibres repeatedly contract. On the box, force × distance = force × 0 = 0 J. Time does not appear in W = F s at all.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the current used up as it flows through a heating element?
items.correct: No. The current is the same all the way round a series circuit; it is energy that is transferred, not current.
items.misconception: The current is used up by the element, which is why the element gets hot and the wire beyond it is cool.
items.why: Something clearly gets 'used' at the element, and current and energy are both invisible, so the two ideas merge. Charge is not consumed. What happens is work done when a current flows, filling the thermal store of the element. Say 'energy is transferred', never 'current is used up'.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why must the bars on an energy diagram share one scale?
items.correct: So that the sizes can be compared and added directly, showing how the total has been redistributed.
items.misconception: Each store can be drawn on its own scale, as long as every bar is labelled with its value.
items.why: In other subjects, charts are drawn to fill the space, and small quantities are often shown on a stretched axis so they can be seen. The specification asks for a common scale precisely so that a small change looks small. Separate scales hide the fact that the amounts before and after must add up to the same total.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: P = E/t. How do you rearrange it to find the energy transferred?
items.correct: E = P t — multiply the power by the time.
items.misconception: You keep the division and write E = P/t, because the equation has a divide in it.
items.why: Rearranging is done by pattern-matching the symbols rather than by doing the same operation to both sides. Multiply both sides by t: P × t = E. Check with units — watts × seconds = joules, whereas watts ÷ seconds is not an energy at all.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.1.1.1 Energy stores and systems
